title: I Logged Every Time the Night ICU Charge Called Me Dramatic

parts.text: I was holding a 3 a.m. saline bag when the charge nurse called me dramatic for the fourth time. I am twenty-nine, ICU, unshockable in a way that bothers people. The waiting room vending machine hummed through the doors. My patient, Mr. Cole, had a family that asked real questions. The charge, Bridget, preferred quiet hallways. "Stop charting so much," she said, snapping gum, wintergreen. "You're scaring the family." I said, "I'm charting because his sats keep dipping." She smiled at the tech. "Dramatic." I wrote wintergreen in the margin of my scrap paper, which is not official, which is why it mattered. At 3:40 she pulled me off the room to restock gloves nobody needed. When I came back, the monitor alarm had been silenced. The family was asleep in chairs that smell like old raincoats. I restored the alarms. Bridget appeared. "I turned those off so people can rest." I said, "People can rest when he's stable." She lowered her voice. "You like being the hero." I like being employed and not sued. I photographed the silenced-alarm audit on the monitor, which logs user IDs if you know the menu. It showed hers. She saw me do it. "That's a HIPAA issue," she said, instantly creative. "False alarms all night. She's new-anxious." I am not new. Dr. Patel looked at the scrap paper in my pocket, the wintergreen notes, like he could smell a fight. Then Mr. Cole's monitor screamed for real, and Bridget's gum went still.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: The alarm she silenced comes back as a real event, and she has already told the attending I am anxious.

social.description: Wintergreen gum, a raincoat-smelling waiting room, and a charge nurse who called charting dramatic. The device log had her user ID. Would you have photographed the audit menu?

parts.text: I was already in the room. Mr. Cole needed oxygen, not a narrative. Dr. Patel moved fast. Bridget tried to take the lead on the story. I said, "Alarms were silenced at 3:40. Log is on the monitor." The wintergreen went in the trash. After the patient stabilized, Dr. Patel asked for the audit. Bridget called it a glitch. The glitch had her ID. I submitted my scrap-paper times with official charting. Risk management likes timestamps more than adjectives like dramatic. Bridget went on a sudden education leave. I hate that phrase. The family brought donuts that tasted like the vending machine's cousin. I still take them. A union rep asked if I wanted to make it bigger. I said, "I want the alarms left on." He nodded. "That's the whole case." They posted a laminated reminder above the monitors, which is both sad and useful. Bridget returned to days. We are civil in the way of people who have seen each other's worst meeting. I keep a cheap notebook in my locker that smells like the alcohol wipes I toss in it so nobody reads it for fun. I wrote one line after that night: hero is a word people use when they want you quiet. Mr. Cole went home. I still hear the vending machine hum when I try to sleep after nights. That is just the building. I can live with buildings. I cannot live with silenced alarms and a smile.
